passage: "Beta, listen to this one," said Naveen, setting down his tea. "When I was your age, in Class 6, we had a maths teacher who never smiled. One day I asked him, 'Sir, why was six afraid of seven?' He said nothing. I said, 'Because seven eight nine!' The whole class exploded. Even Sir's moustache twitched. After that I collected riddles in a notebook and told one at every recess. The boys who used to ignore me started saving me a seat." Suraj groaned, then grinned. "Dadu, that's the same joke you told last Diwali!" "Good jokes never retire," Naveen said, and started another.

qa.q: What did young Naveen ask his maths teacher?
qa.a: He asked, "Sir, why was six afraid of seven?" and gave the answer, "Because seven eight nine!"

qa.q: What did Naveen want when he began collecting riddles in a notebook?
qa.a: He seems to have wanted to share fun and belong, since he told one at every recess and the boys who ignored him began saving him a seat.

qa.q: What could Suraj do to try his own wordplay with his grandfather?
qa.a: Suraj could invent a pun of his own, or trade riddles with Naveen at teatime, so the two of them can enjoy a new joke together.

qa.q: How might the strict teacher have seen Naveen's joke?
qa.a: His moustache twitched, so he may have been amused even though he never smiled. He might also have been surprised that a quiet boy dared to joke with him.

grounding: An elder recalls how a school-age child's pun and riddle habit showed playful language awareness and a wish to be part of the group.

passage: The power cut hit during the school bus breakdown, and thirty kids sat sweating in the dark on the roadside. Divyansh could hear Class 4 getting restless. "Okay, riddle time," he called, torch pointing at his own chin. "What has hands but can't clap?" Silence. Then Mohit yelled, "A clock!" and the whole row cheered. "What's a cat's favourite colour?" "Purr-ple!" someone shouted, and even the conductor laughed. Divyansh's voice had gone hoarse, but he kept the puns coming until the replacement bus arrived, and Mohit kept clapping for each one. 😄

qa.q: What was the answer Mohit shouted to the riddle about hands?
qa.a: Mohit shouted, "A clock!"

qa.q: What was Divyansh probably feeling as he kept telling puns in the dark?
qa.a: He was probably enjoying the shared fun and wanting to keep the group cheerful, shown by his continuing until his voice went hoarse. He might also have been a little nervous himself and used jokes to calm down.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do if his voice gives out before the bus arrives?
qa.a: He could hand the torch to Mohit or another child to ask the next riddle, so the game continues and everyone joins in.

qa.q: How might Mohit and the other children feel about the riddles during the wait?
qa.a: The riddles turn a long, sweaty wait into a game, so Mohit and the others probably feel less restless and more like one group.

grounding: A school-age child uses puns and riddles under a constraint (power cut, broken-down bus) to share fun and hold the group together.

passage:
The birthday party on the fourth floor was loud with older girls from Sharmila's class, and Rukmini stood near the balloons holding a paper cup she had not drunk from.
When the cake was finished, someone said, "Anyone know a good joke?"
Rukmini's cheeks went warm. "Why couldn't the bicycle stand up on its own?"
Nobody knew.
"Because it was two-tired!"
For a second, silence. Then Sharmila groaned, "Nooo, that's terrible," and flopped on the sofa laughing. Two girls repeated it to each other: "Two-tired, too tired!"
"I have one about a cheese too," Rukmini said, a little louder.
"Go on then," Sharmila said, moving her feet so Rukmini could sit.
By the time the auto came, Rukmini had told six riddles and was sitting in the middle of the sofa.

qa.q: How many riddles had Rukmini told by the time the auto came?
qa.a: Rukmini had told six riddles.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini tell the bicycle riddle, and how do her cheeks and cup hint at her mood?
qa.a: She probably wanted to join the older girls: the untouched cup and warm cheeks suggest she felt shy and nervous at first, and sharing a joke was a way in. She may also simply have loved that riddle and wanted someone to hear it.

qa.q: What made the riddle work as a way into the group?
qa.a: It was short, depended on a double meaning everyone could catch, and gave the others something to repeat and groan at together.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen Rukmini before and after the joke?
qa.a: Before, Rukmini was probably just a quiet guest by the balloons; after the pun, Sharmila treated her as part of the fun and made room on the sofa.

grounding: The party shows a school-age child using a pun based on a double meaning to share fun and become part of a group.

"Didi, Didi, what has hands but can't clap?"
Usha didn't look up from her maths. "A clock. You asked me yesterday."
"Okay, okay, new one. I made it myself." Arnab climbed onto the bed. "Why is the ceiling fan a good friend?"
"Arnab, I have twelve sums."
"Because it's always your FAN!" He spread his arms. "Get it? Fan, like it goes round, and fan, like it likes you!"
Usha put her pencil down. "That's... actually not bad."
"Really?"
"Who taught you that?"
"Nobody. I was lying under it and thinking." Arnab grinned. "Tomorrow I'll tell it in class."
"Tell it after the prayer, when Sir is in a good mood."
"Will you be my fan?"
Usha threw a pillow at him, laughing. "Go. Sums."

qa.q: What did Arnab say he was doing when he thought of the fan joke?
qa.a: He said he was lying under the fan and thinking.

qa.q: How can you tell Arnab felt proud of his joke?
qa.a: He announced he made it himself, spread his arms for the punchline, explained both meanings of "fan", and asked "Really?" when Usha praised it, which shows he felt proud and eager for her approval. 😊

qa.q: What advice did Usha give, and why might it help?
qa.a: She suggested telling it after prayer when the teacher is in a good mood, which helps Arnab share his fun at a moment the group is ready to enjoy it.

qa.q: What was it like for Usha to be interrupted during her sums?
qa.a: At first she was a bit impatient because she had twelve sums, but the original pun surprised her and she ended up laughing with him.

grounding: A school-age child invents his own double-meaning pun, showing growing awareness of words and a wish to share fun.

passage:
My first week at the hostel in the hills, I didn't know anybody. I ate fast and went back to my bunk.
On the fourth evening, Dolma leaned over from the next bed. "Knock knock."
I stared at her. "Who's there?"
"Lettuce."
"Lettuce who?"
"Lettuce in, it's freezing out here!"
Half the dorm laughed. I didn't, because I was too busy thinking about how one word could be two words at once.
The next night I was ready. "Knock knock," I said to Dolma. My voice shook a little.
"Who's there?"
"Tank."
"Tank who?"
"You're welcome!"
Dolma laughed so loudly the warden knocked on the door. After that, the whole row of bunks swapped jokes before lights out, and I was in the middle of it.
- Pranav

qa.q: What word did Dolma use in her knock-knock joke?
qa.a: Lettuce.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling when saying the first knock-knock joke?
qa.a: Pranav was probably nervous, since the voice shook, but also hopeful of joining in; staying quiet at Dolma's joke may have been curiosity about the wordplay rather than not finding it funny.

qa.q: What would you advise a new child who feels left out in a hostel?
qa.a: Try sharing something small and fun, like a joke or riddle, with one friendly person first; it can open the door to the whole group.

qa.q: How might Dolma have seen Pranav's first joke?
qa.a: Dolma likely felt pleased that the quiet newcomer had answered her game with a joke of their own, and her loud laugh welcomed Pranav in.

grounding: Looking back, the narrator shows wordplay jokes as both a sign of noticing double meanings and a way to join a group.

Class 4B observation note, Friday
During wet-weather break, Francis stood on the bench and asked, "Why did the maths book look sad? It had too many problems!" Half the class groaned; Binita laughed so hard she hiccuped. Francis beamed and tried another: "What has hands but can't clap?" Binita shouted "A clock!" before he finished, and he looked delighted rather than cross that she knew it. Later I saw the two of them writing riddles in the back of Binita's notebook, hunting for words with two meanings, like "bark" and "bat". Francis is usually quiet in group work, so this felt new. Next step: I have asked them to run a five-minute riddle corner on Monday.

qa.q: Which words with two meanings were Francis and Binita using?
qa.a: "Bark" and "bat".

qa.q: Why did Francis look delighted when Binita knew the answer?
qa.a: He felt pleased and included, because sharing the joke with someone who got it mattered more to him than stumping her 😄

qa.q: What did the note-writer plan next, and why might it help?
qa.a: The teacher asked them to run a riddle corner on Monday, giving Francis, who is usually quiet in groups, a happy way to join in.

qa.q: How might Binita experience Francis's riddles?
qa.a: Binita seemed to enjoy them and feel like a partner in the fun: laughing, answering fast and writing new riddles together.

grounding: It shows a school-age child enjoying puns and riddles built on double meanings as a way to share fun and connect with the group.
